extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and researchers interested in David Foster Wallace and contemporary American literature
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts evaluative and prescriptive features of David Foster Wallace's fiction and nonfiction style as described on his Wikipedia page (e.g., use/avoidance of irony, narrative structure, endnotes, thematic aims). Useful for literary analysis or emulation of Wallace's techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of postmodern tropes (irony, metafiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wallace intentionally avoided tropes of postmodern art such as irony or forms of metafiction, saying in 1990 that they were "agents of a great despair and stasis" in contemporary American culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In essays (notably "E Unibus Pluram") he argued that irony and ridicule, while entertaining and effective, contribute to cultural despair and stasis and pose problems for aspiring fictionists; this frames a criterion to minimize or move beyond ironic/metafictional distance in order to pursue other aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embrace of earnest, unself-conscious experience (New Sincerity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wallace tended to focus on individual persons' continued longing for earnest, unself-conscious experience and communication in a media-saturated society and sought to write "morally passionate, passionately moral fiction".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: His stated aim was to help the reader "become less alone inside." In his Kenyon College address (``This Is Water'') he emphasized attention, awareness, discipline, compassion, and mindfulness as ethical/esthetic commitments — a standard for fiction aiming for emotional sincerity and ethical engagement rather than ironic detachment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unconventional narrative structure and extensive use of endnotes/footnotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Infinite Jest is known for its unconventional narrative structure and extensive use of endnotes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wallace explained that notes were used "to disrupt the linear narrative, to reflect his perception of reality without jumbling the narrative structure" and that he could have jumbled sentences but that would have made the text unreadable. This indicates a technique: use paratextual notes to complicate narrative flow while preserving readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining narrative modes, voices, jargon, and invented vocabulary
rubrics_metrics.description: Wallace's fiction combines narrative modes and authorial voices that incorporate jargon and invented vocabulary, such as self-generated abbreviations and acronyms, long, multi-clause sentences, and an extensive use of explanatory endnotes and footnotes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited include Infinite Jest and the story "Octet"; the combination functions to render complex perspectives and register different social/institutional voices. This is a stylistic criterion: mix registers and coin terms to achieve particular effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporation of philosophical and mathematical ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Much of Wallace's writing contains philosophical and mathematical ideas and references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: His background (modal logic, a philosophy thesis, works like Everything and More) informs writing that weaves conceptual, technical material into literary form — a standard for intellectual density and thematic depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multiple protagonists, expansive settings, and fragmentation
rubrics_metrics.description: His work often features multiple protagonists and spans different locations in a single work; his writing comments on the fragmentation of thought and explores relationships between happiness and boredom and psychological tensions between beauty and hideousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: D. T. Max described Wallace's work as an "unusual mixture of the cerebral and the hot-blooded." This implies a narrative strategy that fragments perspective and setting to mirror psychic or cultural fragmentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tension in nonfiction between vivid scene/characterization and factual reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Some writers have found parts of Wallace's nonfiction implausible; Jonathan Franzen said Wallace made up dialogue and incidents, and John Cook remarked on the temptation to "shave, embellish, and invent narratives."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This raises an evaluative criterion for Wallace-style nonfiction: vivid, pitch-perfect characterization and comic situations may risk factual embellishment. For nonfiction practice, this text foregrounds a tension between literary vivacity and journalistic accuracy.
